studies.finding: Mothers aged 21 to 27 who found mothering satisfying had high ego resiliency; negative experiences were linked to decreased resiliency.

studies.title: Ego resiliency in Dutch children (Smeekens et al., 2007)
studies.finding: Five-year-olds low in ego resiliency showed greater physiological stress during negative interactions with parents.

studies.title: Longitudinal ego development (Block & Block, 2006)
studies.finding: Ego control and ego resiliency were generally stronger in later life than in childhood (ages 3 to 23), and individual differences appeared early.

studies.title: Catharsis and the punching bag (Bushman, Baumeister & Stack, 1999)
studies.finding: Insulted students who read a pro-catharsis message hit a punching bag more and then acted more aggressively, even toward innocent people; venting did not reduce anger.

studies.title: Meta-analysis of displaced aggression (Marcus-Newhall et al., 2000)
studies.finding: Across 97 studies displaced aggression was reliable and more intense in more negative, stressful settings.

studies.title: Brooding and displaced aggression (Bushman et al., 2005)
studies.finding: Provoked students who spent 25 minutes dwelling on their anger showed more displaced aggression.

studies.title: Shock-paired word lists (Glucksberg & King, 1967)
studies.finding: Subjects forgot words accompanied by shock and conceptually similar words on a second list, supporting repression.

studies.title: Repressors vs non-repressors (Davis, 1987)
studies.finding: Repressors recalled fewer negative childhood memories, avoided threatening pictures, and showed physiological but not verbal arousal to sexual or aggressive phrases.

studies.title: Repressors and a disturbing film (Boden & Baumeister, 1997)
studies.finding: After a grisly film, repressors recalled more happy memories, coping with negative stimuli by accessing positive ones.

studies.title: Repression in chronically ill children (Phipps & Steele, 2002)
studies.finding: Children with cancer or chronic illness were more likely to be repressors and less likely to express anger than healthy children.

studies.title: Projection of blame (Rucker & Pratkanis, 2001)
studies.finding: Accusing another of lying and cheating increased blame on them and reduced self-blame for the same behaviour.

studies.title: Projection onto spouses (Schul & Vinokur, 2000)
studies.finding: Unemployed job seekers projected their depression onto partners, more so when partners were actually similar.

studies.title: Hierarchy of defenses (Tallandini & Caudek, 2010; Porcerelli et al., 1998)
studies.finding: Simple defenses like denial are used mostly by young children and decline with age; complex ones like identification increase.

studies.title: Preschool personality and adult denial (Cramer & Block, 1998)
studies.finding: Men still using denial at 23 had shown emotional immaturity and low competence and ego resiliency in nursery school; no clear link for women.

studies.title: Defenses in Americans and Thai Buddhists (Tori & Bilmes, 2002)
studies.finding: The two cultures were strongly similar in use of regression, reaction formation, projection, repression, denial and compensation.

studies.title: War-related dreams in Germany (Schredl & Piel, 2006)
studies.finding: Germans directly affected by World War II still had highly emotional war-related dreams more than 50 years later.

studies.title: Smell and dreams (Hutson, 2010)
studies.finding: Ten seconds of rose scent during sleep produced more pleasant dreams than the smell of rotten eggs.

studies.title: Dreams and well-being (Pesant & Zadra, 2006)
studies.finding: Canadians with lower well-being dreamed more of aggression, negative emotion and failure; those with higher well-being dreamed of friendly interaction and success.

studies.title: Decoding dream images (Horikawa et al., 2013)
studies.finding: Computers learned to decode dream images from brain activity with about 66 percent accuracy.

studies.title: Oedipal behaviour in children (Watson & Getz, 1990)
studies.finding: Children aged 3 to 6 showed more affection to the opposite-sex parent and aggression to the same-sex parent, peaking around 4 and declining by 5.

studies.title: Dreams of castration anxiety and penis envy (Hall & Van de Castle, 1965)
studies.finding: More men reported castration-anxiety dreams; more women reported castration-wish or penis-envy dreams.

studies.title: Ambivalence toward fathers (Maio, Fincham & Lycett, 2000)
studies.finding: Welsh 12- to 14-year-olds ambivalent toward their fathers showed less secure attachment to others.

studies.title: Oral personality and obesity (Masling, Rabie & Blondheim, 1967)
studies.finding: Oral orientation measured by the Rorschach was strongly related to obesity.

studies.title: Oral vs anal conformity (Tribich & Messer, 1974)
studies.finding: Oral types conformed more to an authority figure's suggestions than anal types.

studies.title: Induced Freudian slips (Motley, 1987)
studies.finding: Men anxious about shock made slips like damn shock; sexually anxious men made slips like nude breasts; controls made no such slips.

studies.title: Recovered memories and fantasy proneness (McNally et al., 2000)
studies.finding: Women reporting recovered abuse memories scored higher on fantasy proneness and dissociation.

studies.title: Suggestive interviews of children (Ceci & Bruck, 1993)
studies.finding: Four years later, a third of children agreed they had been hugged and kissed by a man who never touched them.

studies.title: False memories via dream interpretation (Mazzoni et al., 1999)
studies.finding: Most Italian students told their dreams reflected repressed childhood trauma later agreed the trauma had happened.

examples.title: Displacement after a bad day
examples.text: A student scolded by a professor cannot answer back, so she snaps at her younger brother at home. The brother is a safer target, but the anger never fully goes away, matching Freud's point that substitutes leave leftover tension.

examples.title: Rationalization after rejection
examples.text: Someone who is not selected for a college team tells friends the coach plays favourites and the team is not that good anyway. The excuse protects self-esteem by blaming something outside the self.

examples.title: Id, ego and superego at exam time
examples.text: The night before an exam, the id wants to keep scrolling reels, the superego insists you must study every page or you are a bad student, and the ego compromises: study for two hours, then a short break.

examples.title: Sublimation in creative work
examples.text: A teenager with strong aggressive feelings channels them into intense sports practice or writing powerful poetry. Freud would see the energy as redirected into socially admired outlets.

examples.title: Preconscious recall
examples.text: You are not thinking of your friend's phone number right now, but if asked you can bring it to mind instantly. That number was sitting in the preconscious.

practice.answer: Cathexis is Freud's term for the investment of psychic energy, the libido of the life instincts, in an object or person. For example, if you like your roommate, your libido is said to be cathected to that person. The concept explains how instinctual energy becomes attached to particular people, objects and activities in the course of development.

practice.q: Distinguish between manifest and latent content of dreams.
practice.answer: In Freud's dream analysis, the manifest content is the actual storyline or events the dreamer experiences and reports. The latent content is the hidden, symbolic meaning behind those events, representing repressed desires, fears and conflicts. The analyst's task is to interpret the latent content from the manifest content, for example reading climbing stairs as a symbol of sexual intercourse.

Fixation is a condition in which part of the libido remains invested in one psychosexual stage because the conflict of that stage was not resolved (excessive frustration) or because needs were so fully satisfied by an indulgent parent (excessive gratification) that the child did not want to move on. Less energy is then available for later stages, and characteristic adult personality types result, such as the oral passive or anal retentive personality.

practice.q: Explain the three types of anxiety proposed by Freud.
practice.answer:
Freud defined anxiety as an objectless fear, a feeling of dread whose source we cannot identify, and considered it fundamental to all neurotic and psychotic behaviour. Its prototype is the birth trauma, when the infant is thrust from the secure womb into a hostile world. Anxiety arises when the ego is strained by the competing demands of the id, reality and the superego, and Freud identified three types.

Reality (objective) anxiety is fear of real dangers in the external world, such as fires, earthquakes or wild animals. It is the original type from which the others derive and is usually adaptive, guiding us to escape danger and fading once the threat passes, though it can become exaggerated, as in someone afraid to leave home.

Neurotic anxiety originates in childhood conflicts between instinctual gratification and reality. Children are punished for openly expressing sexual or aggressive impulses, so the wish to satisfy id impulses itself comes to trigger anxiety. It is an unconscious fear of punishment for id-dominated behaviour, a conflict between the id and the ego.

Moral anxiety is a conflict between the id and the superego, essentially fear of one's own conscience. When we want to act against our moral code, the superego punishes us with shame or guilt. People with a strict superego experience more moral anxiety.

All three serve as warnings that the ego is threatened; if rational coping fails, the ego turns to defense mechanisms.

practice.q: Describe the oral and anal stages of psychosexual development and the adult personality types associated with fixation at each.
practice.answer:
Freud held that children pass through stages each defined by an erogenous zone and a conflict; unresolved conflict or overindulgence leads to fixation and a lasting character type.

Oral stage (birth to the second year). The mouth is the main source of pleasure through sucking, biting and swallowing, and the infant depends totally on the mother. In the oral incorporative mode the infant takes in pleasurable stimulation; fixation leads to adult preoccupation with eating, drinking, smoking and kissing. Overindulged infants become oral passive personalities: optimistic, dependent, gullible and overly trusting. The oral aggressive or sadistic mode appears with painful teething, when the infant comes to hate as well as love the mother; fixation here produces pessimism, hostility, argumentativeness, sarcastic 'biting' remarks, envy and exploitation of others. The stage ends at weaning.

Anal stage (around 18 months; ages 1 to 3 in Table 2.2). Toilet training is the first interference with instinctual gratification, and the child learns it can defy or please its parents. A child who defecates whenever the parents do not want may develop an anal aggressive personality: cruel, destructive, disorderly and prone to tantrums, treating people as possessions. A child who withholds feces to gain pleasure and attention may develop an anal retentive personality: stubborn, stingy, hoarding, rigid, compulsively neat and overly conscientious.

Research gives some support to oral and anal types, for example links between oral orientation and obesity (Masling et al., 1967) and greater conformity in oral types (Tribich & Messer, 1974).

practice.q: Discuss the criticisms made of Freud's case study method.
practice.answer:
Freud's main research method was the case study, and the chapter identifies several weaknesses.

First, the method itself is not objective or systematic, and the psychoanalytic session cannot be repeated or verified. Childhood conditions cannot be varied, nor home environments recreated in a laboratory.

Second, the data were problematic. Freud kept no verbatim records and wrote notes from memory hours after sessions, so his data may be incomplete and selectively remembered to fit his theory. He rarely checked patients' stories with friends or relatives, so even accurate notes might not reflect true events.

Third, critics argue Freud inferred or even suggested seduction stories. Kihlstrom noted that although Freud claimed nearly all his women patients reported seduction by fathers, his notes show no such claim; others suggest he implanted memories through suggestion.

Fourth, his sample was small and unrepresentative: himself and about a dozen detailed cases, mostly young, unmarried, upper-class, educated women.

Fifth, published cases did not always match his notes; the Rat Man case showed a lengthened analysis, wrong sequence of events and unsupported claims of cure, and Freud destroyed most patient files.

Finally, Freud distrusted experimentation, insisting only analysts could judge his work. The book concludes that his ideas may still have merit, but they must be accepted on some basis other than experimental verification.

practice.q: Explain Freud's structure of personality. How do the id, ego and superego interact?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Freud first described personality in terms of three levels of awareness (conscious, preconscious and unconscious) but later replaced this with three structures: the id, the ego and the superego. The id roughly corresponds to the unconscious, although the ego and superego also have unconscious parts. Personality, in this model, is a dynamic system in which these three structures constantly compete, and the outcome of their conflict shapes behaviour and anxiety.

The id. The id is the reservoir of the instincts and of libido, and it supplies all the psychic energy for the other two structures, which makes it the most powerful part of personality. Directly tied to bodily needs, it operates by the pleasure principle, seeking to increase pleasure and avoid pain by reducing tension immediately. It cannot tolerate delay and has no awareness of reality or of other people's wishes; Freud described it as selfish, primitive, amoral, insistent and rash. Like a hungry newborn who cries but cannot find food, the id can satisfy needs only through reflexes and wish-fulfilling fantasy or hallucination, called primary-process thought.

The ego. As children grow, they learn they cannot grab what they want or vent sexual and aggressive urges whenever they like. They develop perception, recognition, judgment and memory, known as secondary-process thought. These rational capacities form the ego, the rational master of personality, which operates by the reality principle. The ego's job is not to block the id but to help it gain satisfaction in realistic and socially acceptable ways, choosing suitable times, places and objects. It delays, postpones or redirects gratification. Freud compared it to a rider who must guide and restrain the raw power of a horse. Importantly, the ego is never independent of the id; it draws its energy from the id and must constantly mediate between the id and reality. It is the ego that keeps a person in a disliked job to support a family.

The superego. The third structure is our internalized morality, learned from parents by about age 5 or 6 through praise, punishment and example. It has two parts: the conscience, made up of behaviours for which the child was punished, and the ego-ideal, made up of behaviours for which the child was praised. Over time these rules are internalized, so rewards and punishments become self-administered and parental control becomes self-control; violating the code, even in thought, brings guilt or shame. The superego is relentless and even cruel in its pursuit of moral perfection. Like the id it is intense, irrational and uncompromising, and it seeks not to delay id impulses but to inhibit them completely, especially sexual and aggressive ones.

Interaction. The three structures pull in different directions: the id presses for satisfaction, the ego tries to delay it to fit reality, and the superego demands morality above all. The ego is caught in the middle, serving three masters, the id, reality and the superego. Freud saw personality as being in constant battle, walking a tightrope between these demands. When the ego is too severely strained, the result is anxiety: neurotic anxiety reflects conflict between id and ego, and moral anxiety reflects conflict between id and superego. To cope, the ego relies on unconscious defense mechanisms. If the ego fails, the id may dominate and the person may become a danger to society.

Conclusion. Freud's structural model offers a vivid picture of inner conflict and explains anxiety and defense. However, the chapter notes that research reviewed by Fisher and Greenberg found the id, ego and superego could not be tested experimentally, and critics complain the concepts are ambiguous: it is unclear whether they are brain structures or processes. Later work, such as Anna Freud's ego psychology and research on ego control and ego resiliency, has nonetheless expanded the importance of the ego.

practice.q: Describe Freud's psychosexual stages of personality development. Critically evaluate the theory in the light of research evidence.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Freud believed adult character develops in childhood through parent-child interactions, as the child seeks pleasure and parents impose reality and morality. From his own memories and his patients' recollections he concluded that personality is largely formed by age 5. He proposed that development passes through psychosexual stages, each defined by an erogenous zone (mouth, anus, genitals) and a conflict that must be resolved. Failure to resolve a conflict, or excessive indulgence, leads to fixation, in which libido remains invested in that stage and produces a characteristic adult personality.

Oral stage (birth to the second year). Pleasure comes from sucking, biting and swallowing, and the mother is the main object of libido; her responses teach the infant whether the world is safe or perilous. The oral incorporative mode leads, with fixation, to preoccupation with eating, drinking, smoking and kissing, and overindulgence produces the dependent, gullible oral passive personality. The oral aggressive or sadistic mode, arising with teething, can produce a hostile, sarcastic, envious and exploitative adult.

Anal stage (about 18 months; 1 to 3 years). Toilet training is the first interference with instinctual pleasure. Defiant defecation can lead to an anal aggressive personality (cruel, destructive, disorderly), while withholding can lead to an anal retentive personality (stubborn, stingy, rigid, compulsively neat).

Phallic stage (4 to 5 years). Pleasure centres on the genitals. In the Oedipus complex, the boy desires his mother and sees his father as a rival; castration anxiety forces him to repress his desire and identify with the father, adopting his superego standards. Girls, in what followers called the Electra complex, turn from mother to father after discovering they lack a penis and develop penis envy; Freud believed girls never fully resolve this, leaving weaker superegos. Poor resolution produces the narcissistic phallic personality.

Latency (5 to puberty) and genital stage (puberty onward). Latency is not a true stage: the sex instinct is dormant and sublimated into school, sports and same-sex friendships. In the genital stage, if no major fixations exist, the person can find satisfaction in love and work.

Evaluation. Research gives the theory mixed support. Fisher and Greenberg found slight support for oral and anal character types, the basic Oedipal triangle and castration anxiety. Oral orientation has been linked to obesity (Masling et al., 1967) and to conformity (Tribich & Messer, 1974), and the anal character seems to resurface under labels like conscientiousness and obsessive-compulsive personality. Watson and Getz (1990) found children aged 3 to 6 showed more affection to the opposite-sex parent and aggression to the same-sex parent, peaking at 4, and Hall and Van de Castle (1965) found sex differences in castration-anxiety and penis-envy dreams. However, most research finds no validity in the Oedipus complex as Freud described it (Kupfersmid, 1995); there is no support for the psychosexual stages as such, for resolution through fearful identification with the father, for women's weaker superegos, or for women being more orally dependent (O'Neill & Bornstein, 1990). There is little evidence for the phallic personality. Crucially, the claim that personality is fixed by age 5 is contradicted: preschool personality changes dramatically (Kagan et al., 1978), middle childhood may matter more, and Kagan concluded temperament and later experience outweigh early parent-child interaction. Critics also reject Freud's views on women and his neglect of later development.

Conclusion. The psychosexual theory was original and influential in emphasising childhood, and parts of it, especially oral and anal character types, have some support. But its central claims about universal stages, the Oedipus complex and the fixity of personality by age 5 are not supported by research.

practice.q: Critically evaluate the contributions and limitations of Freud's psychoanalysis, including the research evidence for his concepts.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Freud's psychoanalysis was the first formal theory of personality and is still the best known. It proposed that behaviour is driven by unconscious instincts, structured by the id, ego and superego, protected by defense mechanisms, and shaped by psychosexual stages in early childhood. An evaluation must weigh its enormous influence against weaknesses in its method and its mixed empirical record.

Contributions. Freud's system has had a phenomenal impact on psychology, psychiatry and popular culture. It stimulated American interest in personality from the 1930s and in motivation in the 1940s and 1950s. Contemporary psychology has absorbed key Freudian ideas: the role of the unconscious, the importance of childhood experience for adult behaviour, and defense mechanisms. His assessment methods, free association and dream analysis, along with concepts such as resistance and latent content, shaped therapy. His theory also stimulated later theorists, both followers like Anna Freud, who developed ego psychology and fully articulated the defense mechanisms, and opponents who built alternatives.

Research support. Several concepts have strong support. Unconscious influence is now well established and may be more pervasive than Freud thought: subliminal stimuli affect associations (Shevrin), goals and behaviour (Bargh et al.), consumption (Winkielman et al.) and emotional processes (Silverman and Weinberger's Mommy and I are one studies). Repression is supported by Glucksberg and King's shock-paired words and by studies of repressors (Davis; Boden & Baumeister). Displacement is reliable across 97 studies (Marcus-Newhall et al.), and projection and denial have been demonstrated, with defenses forming a developmental hierarchy. Freudian slips have been induced experimentally (Motley), dreams do reflect emotional concerns, and oral and anal character types have some support. Research on ego control and ego resiliency has extended the concept of the ego and links it to adjustment and well-being.

Limitations. Fisher and Greenberg found the id, ego, superego, death wish, libido and anxiety untestable. Dreams as wish fulfilment, the psychosexual stages, the Oedipus complex as described, and women's weaker superegos are not supported. Catharsis is contradicted: venting anger increases aggression (Bushman et al.). Personality continues to develop after age 5 (Kagan). Research on recovered memories shows false memories can be implanted (Ceci & Bruck; Mazzoni et al.; Loftus). Methodologically, Freud's case studies were unsystematic and unverifiable, based on notes written from memory, a small unrepresentative sample of mostly upper-class young women, and published cases that differed from his notes, as in the Rat Man case. Freud also dismissed experimental tests. Other theorists criticise his overemphasis on biology, sex and aggression, his determinism, his focus on the past rather than future goals, his concentration on disturbed rather than healthy people, his negative views of women, and the ambiguity of concepts like id, ego and superego. As therapy, psychoanalysis has declined in the United States because of its cost and length, the rise of brief therapy and drugs, and managed care's demand for evidence, though it has grown in China and online.

Conclusion. Freud's theory is more influential than his therapy, and many specific claims have not survived testing. Yet his insights into the unconscious, defenses and the importance of childhood remain central to psychology. As the chapter concludes, by giving later theorists an original and challenging foundation to build on or argue against, Freud secured his place in the history of personality theory.

flashcards.front: How does sublimation differ from displacement?
flashcards.back: Displacement changes the object of an impulse; sublimation alters the impulse itself into socially acceptable activity. Sublimation is a form of displacement.

flashcards.front: What is fixation?
flashcards.back: Libido remaining invested in a psychosexual stage because of excessive frustration or gratification.

flashcards.front: Traits of the oral aggressive (oral sadistic) personality?
flashcards.back: Pessimism, hostility, aggressiveness, sarcastic 'biting' remarks, envy, exploiting and dominating others.

flashcards.front: Traits of the anal retentive personality?
flashcards.back: Stubborn, stingy, hoarding, rigid, compulsively neat, obstinate and overly conscientious.

flashcards.front: Where does the name Oedipus complex come from?
flashcards.back: Sophocles' play Oedipus Rex, in which Oedipus unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother.

flashcards.front: What is castration anxiety?
flashcards.back: A boy's fear during the Oedipal period that his father will cut off his penis.

flashcards.front: What did Freud believe resulted from girls never fully resolving the female Oedipus complex?
flashcards.back: Poorly developed superegos in women.

flashcards.front: Why is latency not a psychosexual stage?
flashcards.back: The sex instinct is dormant, sublimated in school, hobbies, sports and same-sex friendships.

flashcards.front: What does the genital personality find satisfaction in?
flashcards.back: Love and work.

flashcards.front: Freud on free will vs determinism?
flashcards.back: Largely deterministic, but psychoanalysis can increase free will by making the unconscious conscious.

flashcards.front: Who influenced Freud's development of free association?
flashcards.back: Josef Breuer, whose hypnosis of a hysterical patient led to catharsis.

flashcards.front: What is resistance?
flashcards.back: A patient's blockage or refusal to disclose painful memories in free association; a sign analysis is near the problem's source.

flashcards.front: What did Fisher and Greenberg's review of 2,500 studies find untestable?
flashcards.back: The id, ego, superego, death wish, libido and anxiety.

flashcards.front: Ego control vs ego resiliency?
flashcards.back: Ego control is the amount of restraint over impulses; ego resiliency is flexibility in adjusting that control to circumstances.

flashcards.front: Does venting anger reduce it, according to research?
flashcards.back: No. Bushman and colleagues found venting increased aggression.

flashcards.front: What did Motley's study show about Freudian slips?
flashcards.back: Shock-anxious men said 'damn shock' and sexually anxious men 'nude breasts', suggesting some slips reveal hidden anxiety.

flashcards.front: What major change did Anna Freud make to psychoanalysis?
flashcards.back: She expanded the ego's role, arguing it operates independently of the id (The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defense, 1936).

summary: Freud's psychoanalysis is the first and best-known formal personality theory, and it is partly autobiographical: it drew on his childhood, his dreams and his sexual conflicts.
Instincts are mental representations of internal bodily needs that drive behaviour to reduce tension (a homeostatic model); displacement of their energy explains the diversity of personality.
Life instincts serve survival, their energy is libido, and investing it in objects is cathexis. Death instincts are an unconscious drive toward decay and aggression.
The mind has conscious, preconscious and unconscious levels; the unconscious is the largest and most powerful (iceberg analogy).

The id (pleasure principle, primary-process thought) supplies all energy. The ego (reality principle, secondary-process thought) mediates. The superego (conscience and ego-ideal) demands moral perfection.
Anxiety, whose prototype is the birth trauma, arises when the ego is overstrained. Reality anxiety is fear of real dangers, neurotic anxiety is id versus ego, and moral anxiety is id versus superego.

Defense mechanisms (repression, denial, reaction formation, projection, regression, rationalization, displacement, sublimation) are unconscious distortions of reality that protect the ego; Freud saw them as necessary for mental health.

The psychosexual stages are oral (incorporative and aggressive modes), anal (toilet training; anal aggressive and retentive types), phallic (Oedipus complex, castration anxiety, penis envy), latency (sublimation) and genital (love and work). Fixation produces lasting character types.

Freud's image of human nature is pessimistic and largely deterministic. The goal of life is tension reduction. Personality is partly inherited (id, stages) and partly learned, and it is universal in its stages but unique in the content of ego and superego.
Assessment uses free association (with resistance as a key sign) and dream analysis (manifest vs latent content), both requiring skilled interpretation.

Freud's case-study method is criticized as unsystematic, unverifiable, based on notes written from memory and on a small unrepresentative sample, and his published cases did not always match his notes.

Research supports unconscious influence, repression, displacement, projection, denial, Freudian slips, dreams reflecting emotional concerns, and some oral/anal traits. It does not support dreams as wish fulfilment, the stages, the Oedipus complex as described, catharsis, or personality being fixed by age 5. False memories can be implanted.
Anna Freud founded ego psychology, arguing the ego works independently of the id, and fully developed the defense mechanisms.

Psychoanalytic therapy has declined in the U.S., and Freud is criticized for overemphasizing biology, sex, the past and pathology, for his determinism, his views on women and his vague concepts. His influence on psychology and culture remains enormous.

assessment.q: Freud's German term for instinct, Trieb, is best translated as:
assessment.explain: The chapter notes that Trieb means a driving force or impulse (Bettelheim, 1984).

assessment.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a need served by the life instincts?
assessment.explain: Life instincts serve needs for food, water, air and sex; destruction belongs to the death instincts.

assessment.q: The idea of the death instincts was received by Freud's followers with:
assessment.explain: The chapter says the death instincts achieved only limited acceptance even among dedicated followers.

assessment.q: Which structure strives for neither pleasure nor realistic goals but solely for moral perfection?
assessment.explain: The superego strives solely for moral perfection, unlike the id (pleasure) and the ego (realistic goals).

assessment.q: A hungry infant who cries and imagines food but cannot obtain it illustrates:
assessment.explain: The id satisfies needs only through reflexes and wish-fulfilling fantasy, which is primary-process thought.

assessment.q: Someone who cannot light a match for fear of fire shows:
options: Reality anxiety carried to an extreme
assessment.explain: The chapter gives this as an example of reality-based fear carried beyond the point of normality.

assessment.q: Which defense involves retreating to an earlier, more secure period of life and behaving in a childish, dependent way?
assessment.explain: Regression is retreating to an earlier, less frustrating stage and displaying that period's behaviour.

assessment.q: According to Freud, why does repeated displacement lead to a build-up of tension?
options: Substitute objects do not reduce tension as well as the original object
assessment.explain: A substitute object does not reduce tension as satisfactorily as the original, so undischarged tension accumulates.

assessment.q: In Table 2.2, which stage is characterised by 'incestuous fantasies; Oedipus complex; anxiety; superego development'?
assessment.explain: Table 2.2 lists these characteristics for the phallic stage (ages 4 to 5).

assessment.q: The anal stage is significant because it involves:
options: The first interference with gratification of an instinctual impulse
The dormancy of the sex instinct
assessment.explain: With toilet training, gratification of an instinctual impulse is interfered with for the first time.

assessment.q: Which personality type does Freud describe as narcissistic and needing constant recognition?
assessment.explain: The phallic personality shows strong narcissism and needs constant recognition and appreciation.

assessment.q: Why did Freud sit behind the couch, out of the patient's sight?
options: Because he disliked being stared at and did not want his expressions to influence patients
assessment.explain: He gave both a personal reason (disliking being stared at) and a professional one (not influencing patients with his expressions).

assessment.q: In Table 2.3 of Freud's dream symbols, 'beginning a journey' signifies:
assessment.explain: Table 2.3 lists beginning a journey as symbolising dying; bathing signifies birth and flying a desire to be admired.

assessment.q: What was the dominant theme of the more than 40 of Freud's own dreams reported in The Interpretation of Dreams?
assessment.explain: Only a few had sexual content; the dominant theme was ambition, which Freud denied having.

assessment.q: In Glucksberg and King's (1967) study, subjects forgot:
options: Words paired with electric shock and conceptually similar words
All words on both lists equally
Only words that were never shocked
assessment.explain: They forgot the shock-paired words and similar words on the second list, supporting repression.

assessment.q: Research on the hierarchy of defense mechanisms shows that, with age:
assessment.explain: Simple defenses like denial are used mainly by young children and decline, while more complex ones like identification increase.

assessment.q: Watson and Getz (1990) found that Oedipal-type behaviours in children were greatest at around age:
assessment.explain: Affection to the opposite-sex parent and aggression to the same-sex parent peaked around age 4 and declined by 5.

assessment.q: Jerome Kagan concluded that personality depends more on:
assessment.explain: Kagan concluded personality depends more on temperament and later childhood than on early parent-child interactions.

assessment.q: Mazzoni et al. (1999) showed that false memories of childhood trauma could be implanted through:
assessment.explain: Italian students told their dreams reflected repressed trauma later came to believe the traumatic events had happened.

assessment.q: Anna Freud's 1936 book considered a basic work of ego psychology is:
options: The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defense
assessment.explain: The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defense (1936) clarified the defenses and is a basic work of ego psychology.
